questions.question: An adult develops new short-term memory impairment and behavioral change over four weeks, followed by unexplained focal seizures. MRI is initially normal. Which interpretation best fits the 2016 clinical framework?
options: Possible autoimmune encephalitis warrants evaluation if alternative causes are reasonably excluded
Definite autoimmune encephalitis is established by the unexplained seizures
Autoimmune encephalitis requires a positive neuronal antibody before clinical classification
Normal MRI places the presentation outside possible autoimmune encephalitis
questions.explanation:
Possible Autoimmune Encephalitis Is a Clinical Entry Point

Correct answer: Possible autoimmune encephalitis warrants evaluation if alternative causes are reasonably excluded

Apply All Parts of the Entry Criteria

**Possible autoimmune encephalitis requires subacute progression over less than three months** of working-memory impairment, altered mental status or psychiatric symptoms.

At least one supporting feature is required: a new focal CNS finding, seizures unexplained by a known seizure disorder, CSF pleocytosis above five cells per cubic millimetre, or MRI features suggesting encephalitis.

Reasonable exclusion of alternative causes is also essential. The criteria are not fulfilled simply because a patient has psychiatric symptoms or responds transiently to steroids.

Classification Guides Investigation, Not Automatic Attribution

**The possible category is an entry point rather than proof of a specific antibody-mediated illness.** Obtain a careful trajectory and exposure history, neurologic assessment, appropriate MRI, EEG and CSF studies.

Investigate infection, seizures themselves, toxic or metabolic disturbance and structural or neoplastic causes according to context. Treat urgent threats while diagnostic assessment proceeds.

Higher-confidence syndrome-specific or antibody-negative probable categories have additional requirements. Treatment decisions integrate severity, objective findings and exclusions; neither waiting indefinitely for antibodies nor treating every possible case as definite disease is justified. Serial assessment can clarify an evolving syndrome and reveal an alternative explanation.

Definite autoimmune encephalitis is established by the unexplained seizures: Seizures support the possible category in a compatible subacute syndrome, but do not independently establish definite autoimmune encephalitis or exclude infectious and other causes.

Autoimmune encephalitis requires a positive neuronal antibody before clinical classification: Antibodies can establish specific syndromes and improve confidence, but the possible category was designed to permit clinical assessment before delayed results are available.

Normal MRI places the presentation outside possible autoimmune encephalitis: MRI abnormalities can support the criteria, but new unexplained seizures provide another qualifying feature; a normal scan does not automatically exclude the possible category.

questions.question: A patient has a convincing evolving encephalitic syndrome with memory loss and new seizures. MRI and initial CSF cell count are normal. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Use normal MRI and CSF to classify antibody-negative probable autoimmune encephalitis
Use the normal CSF cell count to prioritize a primary psychiatric diagnosis
Use normal MRI to establish a toxic-metabolic encephalopathy
Continue a phenotype-directed evaluation; normal routine results do not exclude autoimmune encephalitis
questions.explanation:
Normal Routine Tests Do Not End a Compatible Evaluation

Correct answer: Continue a phenotype-directed evaluation; normal routine results do not exclude autoimmune encephalitis

Sensitivity Varies With Syndrome and Timing

**Autoimmune encephalitis can have normal conventional MRI or little routine CSF inflammation.** Early testing, the underlying antibody syndrome and the sequence of manifestations influence what is detected.

Review the actual MRI sequences and timing and reassess when clinical evolution warrants it. EEG can detect seizures or focal dysfunction even when structural imaging is unrevealing.

A normal result is therefore a limitation to interpret, not permission to ignore the patient’s trajectory. Conversely, nonspecific EEG slowing alone does not prove immune inflammation.

Seek Converging Evidence and Revisit Mimics

**Select further tests from the clinical phenotype**, including appropriately interpreted neural antibodies and infectious studies rather than indiscriminate panels detached from the syndrome.

Review medicines, intoxication, metabolic abnormalities, sleep, ongoing seizures and possible malignancy. An alternative cause may coexist with an antibody or mimic one part of the presentation.

Maintain diagnostic confidence proportional to the evidence. Normal routine studies do not mandate immunotherapy, while serious progressive disease may justify treatment after appropriate exclusion work without every test becoming abnormal. Document the unresolved questions, safety monitoring and reassessment plan so that both treatment response and new discordant findings receive critical review.

Use normal MRI and CSF to classify antibody-negative probable autoimmune encephalitis: That category requires positive supporting evidence and relevant exclusions; the absence of routine abnormalities neither establishes probable disease nor excludes all autoimmune syndromes.

Use the normal CSF cell count to prioritize a primary psychiatric diagnosis: A primary psychiatric disorder remains a differential, but a normal cell count cannot explain away objective seizures and an evolving cognitive syndrome or exclude autoimmune disease.

Use normal MRI to establish a toxic-metabolic encephalopathy: Metabolic and toxic causes need active investigation, but normal structural imaging is not specific for them and does not establish the mechanism.

questions.question: A young adult has an encephalitic syndrome with psychiatric change, seizures and abnormal movements. Serum NMDAR antibody testing is negative. Which testing strategy is most appropriate when lumbar puncture is safe?
options: Obtain serum IgM and IgA NMDAR antibodies to improve diagnostic sensitivity
Repeat serum IgG GluN1 testing using another assay before considering CSF
Obtain CSF total IgG index and use it as the specific confirmatory test
Obtain CSF IgG GluN1 testing with paired serum/CSF interpretation
questions.explanation:
Choose the Specimen as Carefully as the Antibody

Correct answer: Obtain CSF IgG GluN1 testing with paired serum/CSF interpretation

Sensitivity Is Antigen- and Specimen-Dependent

**Paired serum and CSF neural antibody testing is often useful**, but the most informative specimen differs by target. CSF is particularly important for NMDAR IgG; serum is more sensitive for LGI1 in many settings.

The relevant NMDAR antibody is IgG against the GluN1 subunit. Other immunoglobulin classes or isolated incongruent serum results should not be equated with the established syndrome.

Collect appropriate samples before immunotherapy when feasible, without creating an unsafe treatment delay. IVIG and other therapies can complicate subsequent interpretation.

An Assay Result Must Fit the Patient

**Integrate antibody findings with the syndrome, test method and alternative diagnoses.** Tissue-based screening and antigen-specific confirmation can help resolve unexpected or discordant results.

A positive commercial panel is not an independent diagnosis, especially at low pretest probability. Seek expert laboratory review if the phenotype and result conflict.

CSF also supports investigation for infection, inflammation and selected neoplastic mimics. A negative serum result should not end the evaluation of a strongly compatible NMDAR presentation, while a positive serum result without supporting clinical evidence should not trigger automatic long-term immunosuppression. Discuss tumor assessment and treatment through a syndrome-specific pathway once the integrated diagnosis is supported.

Obtain serum IgM and IgA NMDAR antibodies to improve diagnostic sensitivity: Other antibody classes have been reported in different contexts, but the established encephalitis association concerns IgG GluN1; substituting classes can mislead attribution.

Repeat serum IgG GluN1 testing using another assay before considering CSF: A second assay can resolve an unexpected result, but a strongly compatible NMDAR syndrome warrants CSF testing because serum alone can be negative.

Obtain CSF total IgG index and use it as the specific confirmatory test: An IgG index can support intrathecal immune activity, but is not antigen-specific and cannot replace CSF GluN1 IgG testing for this syndrome.

questions.question: A patient with years of nonspecific fatigue and subjective cognitive symptoms has a weak serum CASPR2 result on a commercial panel. Examination, MRI and routine CSF are unrevealing, without seizures or peripheral hyperexcitability. What is the best next step?
options: Repeat serum CASPR2 titres and treat if the result remains positive
Begin a monitored IVIG trial and use objective cognition as its endpoint
Reassess the phenotype and discuss confirmatory testing with the laboratory before immune attribution
Obtain FDG-PET as the decisive confirmation of autoimmune encephalitis
questions.explanation:
A Positive Panel Does Not Establish the Mechanism

Correct answer: Reassess the phenotype and discuss confirmatory testing with the laboratory before immune attribution

Pretest Probability Changes the Meaning of Positivity

**Clinical compatibility is essential when interpreting a neural antibody.** Weak isolated serum results can be unrelated to symptoms, especially when broad testing is applied to a low-probability presentation.

CASPR2-associated disease has recognizable central and peripheral phenotypes, including limbic dysfunction, neuromyotonia and Morvan syndrome. Years of nonspecific symptoms without such findings provide weaker support.

Check the actual antigen, specimen, assay and reported level rather than interpreting the word positive as a diagnosis. Laboratory confirmation can include an orthogonal method or referral testing appropriate to the analyte.

Reassess Before Escalating Treatment

**Seek an explanation for the patient’s symptoms while reviewing diagnostic confidence.** Sleep disorders, medicines, mood, metabolic disease and other neurologic conditions may warrant targeted assessment.

Do not regard a normal MRI as proof against all autoimmune disease; the concern here is the combined chronic nonspecific phenotype and discordant laboratory evidence.

Record why the result is or is not considered clinically relevant and discuss uncertain findings with the testing service. Avoid using either subjective steroid benefit or repeated panel positivity as a substitute for objective syndrome assessment. A subsequent compatible evolution should prompt reassessment rather than permanent dismissal, while unsupported immunotherapy can expose the patient to harm and delay the correct diagnosis.

Repeat serum CASPR2 titres and treat if the result remains positive: Repeat testing may clarify reproducibility, but persistent weak positivity does not independently establish that the symptoms arise from CASPR2 autoimmunity.

Begin a monitored IVIG trial and use objective cognition as its endpoint: An objective treatment trial can be appropriate in sufficiently supported immune disease, but this weak phenotype-incongruent result first requires confirmation and reassessment of alternatives.

Obtain FDG-PET as the decisive confirmation of autoimmune encephalitis: PET can contribute in selected unresolved cases, but nonspecific metabolic abnormalities cannot resolve an incongruent antibody result or replace the clinical diagnostic framework.

questions.question: An adult has fever, confusion, new seizures and temporal-lobe MRI abnormalities. Initial CSF studies and neuronal antibodies are pending. Which diagnostic-treatment approach is most appropriate?
options: Obtain CSF neural antibodies first and reserve pathogen testing for a negative panel
Begin IVIG while using repeat MRI to determine whether antiviral coverage is needed
Investigate infectious and immune causes in parallel while promptly covering plausible HSV encephalitis
Use CSF cell count and protein to choose exclusively between antiviral and immune treatment
questions.explanation:
Exclude Infection Before an Immune Attribution

Correct answer: Investigate infectious and immune causes in parallel while promptly covering plausible HSV encephalitis

Shared Phenotypes Require Parallel Investigation

**Infectious and autoimmune encephalitis overlap clinically.** Fever, seizures, altered behavior and temporal MRI changes are not unique to either mechanism.

Obtain CSF when safe for cell count, glucose, protein and relevant pathogen studies, including HSV PCR, alongside phenotype-directed neural antibody testing. Review MRI and EEG in context.

Investigate toxic, metabolic, vascular and neoplastic alternatives when the history or findings suggest them. A positive neural antibody would not automatically exclude coincident infection.

Time-Sensitive Care Precedes Complete Certainty

**Give appropriate empiric antimicrobial treatment for a plausible infectious encephalitis.** HSV-active intravenous therapy should follow renal-adjusted local protocols, with hydration and kidney monitoring.

An early negative HSV PCR can require repeat testing when suspicion remains high; integrate sample timing, imaging and clinical evolution rather than stopping therapy on one isolated result.

Consider immune treatment after appropriate infectious assessment when the integrated syndrome supports it, without waiting indefinitely for antibody results. A mass-like lesion requiring lymphoma or other tissue diagnosis introduces separate steroid considerations. The key decision is to protect against a treatable infection while building evidence for mechanism, not to force the case into an immune category from one imaging feature.

Obtain CSF neural antibodies first and reserve pathogen testing for a negative panel: A sequential antibody-first strategy can delay a time-sensitive infection diagnosis; infection and immune testing should proceed together when both are plausible.

Begin IVIG while using repeat MRI to determine whether antiviral coverage is needed: IVIG can treat supported immune disease, but repeat imaging cannot safely gate prompt antiviral treatment in a plausible acute HSV presentation.

Use CSF cell count and protein to choose exclusively between antiviral and immune treatment: Routine CSF findings overlap and do not reliably establish one mechanism; targeted pathogen tests, clinical context and appropriate empiric cover remain necessary.

questions.explanation:
Antibody-Independent Definite Limbic Encephalitis

Correct answer: Definite autoimmune limbic encephalitis

Meet the Defined Limbic Framework

**Definite autoimmune limbic encephalitis can be diagnosed using a compatible subacute syndrome**, bilateral medial temporal T2/FLAIR abnormalities highly restricted to those regions, supporting CSF or EEG evidence, and reasonable exclusion of other causes.

The clinical syndrome develops within less than three months and includes working-memory deficits, seizures or psychiatric symptoms suggesting limbic involvement.

Support consists of CSF pleocytosis above five cells per cubic millimetre or temporal epileptic/slow-wave EEG activity. Both tests do not have to be abnormal when the rest of this framework is met.

Bilateral Signal Is Important but Not Self-Sufficient

**HSV infection, seizure-related changes and neoplastic processes can mimic parts of the picture.** The exclusion requirement remains necessary even when the medial temporal pattern is striking.

Unilateral temporal abnormalities alone do not meet this antibody-independent definite framework; such patients can still have antibody-associated disease and need further evaluation.

Test for relevant neural antibodies because they inform mechanism, tumor association and treatment planning even when classification is already supported clinically. Negative tests do not eliminate all cancer risk or replace an appropriate tumor assessment. Conversely, the term limbic encephalitis does not establish that any coincident tumor is causative; correlate the phenotype, antibody and cancer evidence before assigning paraneoplastic certainty.

Probable antibody-negative autoimmune encephalitis: This category addresses cases outside well-defined autoimmune syndromes; the patient already meets the defined antibody-independent definite limbic framework.

Definite paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis: A paraneoplastic mechanism requires relevant cancer and integrated PNS evidence; a limbic syndrome does not independently establish that association.

questions.explanation:
EEG Supports the Syndrome and Detects Treatable Seizures

Correct answer: Slowing documents dysfunction but is nonspecific; consider longer monitoring if nonconvulsive seizures remain plausible

EEG Has Diagnostic and Monitoring Roles

**Use EEG to identify seizures, nonconvulsive status and cerebral dysfunction.** A clinical episode can reflect seizures, movement phenomena, dysautonomia, medicines or the encephalopathy itself.

Correlate observed events with the recording where possible. Continuous or longer monitoring is appropriate when fluctuating awareness or unexplained deterioration creates ongoing concern.

Diffuse slowing is nonspecific; temporal abnormalities can support a limbic syndrome but also occur with infection, structural disease and seizure-related injury.

Recognize Patterns Without Making Them a Standalone Diagnosis

**Extreme delta brush is associated with NMDAR encephalitis**, but the EEG must be interpreted alongside the phenotype, CSF and relevant antibody findings.

Superimposed fast activity can also be influenced by medicines. Not every abnormal movement is an electrographic seizure, and not every unusual EEG pattern calls for anesthetic suppression.

Treat confirmed seizures and status promptly while continuing evaluation of the underlying mechanism. A brief study with no seizure does not guarantee that a later event is nonictal. Reassess sedation, metabolic abnormalities and infection when interpreting background changes; objective seizure control and recovery of cognition may follow different time courses, so one should not be used as a simple surrogate for the other.

Use the background slowing as the principal evidence for immune escalation: Slowing can help characterize dysfunction, but infection, medicines and metabolic causes also produce it; immune escalation needs the integrated disease assessment.

Attribute the episodes to the encephalopathy and follow with routine EEG at discharge: Encephalopathy can cause fluctuations, but a short recording may miss intermittent seizures; persistent clinical concern warrants timely longer monitoring rather than delayed reassessment.

Escalate antiseizure treatment solely to normalize diffuse slowing: Diffuse slowing reflects nonspecific dysfunction and is not itself an ictal target; treatment escalation should address seizures or another defined indication.

questions.question: A previously well young adult develops rapidly progressive behavioral change, markedly reduced speech, seizures, orofacial dyskinesias and episodes of autonomic instability over three weeks. Which antibody-associated syndrome best unifies this evolution?
options: NMDAR encephalitis
LGI1 encephalitis
CASPR2-associated Morvan syndrome
GABA-B receptor encephalitis
questions.explanation:
An Evolving NMDAR Syndrome

Correct answer: NMDAR encephalitis

Recognize the Multidomain Evolution

**NMDAR encephalitis can evolve across psychiatric, cognitive, speech, seizure, movement and autonomic domains.** Central hypoventilation and reduced consciousness can complicate severe disease.

Symptoms need not begin simultaneously. An initial psychiatric presentation can precede objective neurologic features; a changing trajectory should trigger reassessment.

Orofacial dyskinesias and complex movements are not all seizures. Video-EEG and bedside correlation help avoid both untreated status and unnecessary deep sedation.

Confirm and Protect Against Acute Complications

**Obtain CSF IgG directed against GluN1**, with paired serum assessment and exclusion of important infectious and other mimics. MRI may be normal despite severe illness.

Assess for associated tumors using an age- and sex-informed strategy, particularly ovarian teratoma where relevant. Absence of a detected tumor does not exclude the diagnosis.

Treat through specialist immune-therapy and supportive pathways, including seizure care and close respiratory and autonomic monitoring when indicated. Evaluate swallowing, aspiration, thrombosis, nutrition and rehabilitation needs during prolonged illness. Recovery can be slow and uneven; persistent cognitive or behavioral difficulties require follow-up rather than being equated automatically with ongoing active inflammation or irreversible decline.

Antibody | High-yield phenotype | Important association or test clue

NMDAR | Psychiatric/speech change, seizures, dyskinesias, dysautonomia | CSF IgG GluN1; ovarian teratoma in relevant patients

LGI1 | Limbic amnesia, focal seizures, FBDS | Hyponatremia; routine CSF may be bland

CASPR2 | Limbic disease or peripheral hyperexcitability/Morvan | Insomnia and dysautonomia; selected thymoma association

GABA-B receptor | Seizure-predominant limbic disease, possible status | Important SCLC association

AMPAR | Limbic cognitive/psychiatric syndrome | Lung, breast and thymic tumors; relapse can occur

LGI1 encephalitis: LGI1 disease often causes limbic memory impairment and focal seizures, including brief faciobrachial events; this prominent speech, dyskinetic and autonomic multisystem evolution is more characteristic of NMDAR disease.

CASPR2-associated Morvan syndrome: Morvan syndrome combines peripheral nerve hyperexcitability, marked sleep disturbance and dysautonomia; those features differ from the predominant speech, seizure and orofacial dyskinetic syndrome here.

GABA-B receptor encephalitis: GABA-B receptor disease often presents with severe seizures and limbic cognitive dysfunction, frequently with relevant cancer risk; the broader young-adult dyskinetic and autonomic phenotype more strongly suggests NMDAR disease.

questions.explanation:
Tumor Assessment Accompanies NMDAR Confirmation

Correct answer: Obtain targeted pelvic imaging and plan risk-informed follow-up

Target the Search to the Syndrome and Patient

**Ovarian teratoma is an important association in adult women with NMDAR encephalitis.** Tumor prevalence varies with age and sex, so one universal screening scheme is inappropriate.

Use suitable pelvic ultrasound or MRI according to the initial study, local expertise and clinical circumstances. Review whether the ovaries were adequately assessed rather than assuming an abdominal report answers every pelvic question.

A negative initial tumor search is not evidence against a well-supported antibody-confirmed neurologic diagnosis.

Combine Tumor and Neurologic Management

**Treat an identified relevant tumor through specialist gynecologic/oncologic care alongside immunotherapy.** Removing a trigger does not eliminate the need for acute neurologic support.

Persistent or relapsing disease should prompt review of tumor assessment, diagnostic confidence and treatment response. Repeat screening is individualized; do not transfer the PNS-Care high-risk-antibody schedule indiscriminately to every NMDAR patient.

Discuss fertility, procedure risks and uncertainty with the patient or appropriate decision-maker. Empirical removal of normal ovaries is not justified merely by a positive antibody. Continue cognitive, psychiatric and functional rehabilitation, because neurologic recovery may lag behind tumor treatment and the disappearance of acute autonomic or seizure complications.

Obtain chest imaging first and reserve ovarian assessment for persistent disease: Chest investigation can be part of a broader search, but the characteristic age/sex-specific ovarian association warrants targeted assessment without waiting for refractory disease.

Repeat abdominal CT after neurologic recovery before obtaining pelvic imaging: Interval systemic imaging can have a role, but a young woman with confirmed NMDAR disease needs adequate targeted ovarian assessment during the current evaluation.

Use whole-body FDG-PET as the definitive exclusion of an ovarian teratoma: PET can assist selected cancer investigations, but cannot be treated as a definitive substitute for appropriate pelvic structural assessment of a suspected teratoma.

Tumor Assessment Accompanies NMDAR Confirmation

Correct answer: C — Obtain targeted pelvic imaging and plan risk-informed follow-up

Target the Search to the Syndrome and Patient

  • Ovarian teratoma is an important association in adult women with NMDAR encephalitis. Tumor prevalence varies with age and sex, so one universal screening scheme is inappropriate.
    • Use suitable pelvic ultrasound or MRI according to the initial study, local expertise and clinical circumstances. Review whether the ovaries were adequately assessed rather than assuming an abdominal report answers every pelvic question.
    • A negative initial tumor search is not evidence against a well-supported antibody-confirmed neurologic diagnosis.

Combine Tumor and Neurologic Management

  • Treat an identified relevant tumor through specialist gynecologic/oncologic care alongside immunotherapy. Removing a trigger does not eliminate the need for acute neurologic support.

    • Discuss fertility, procedure risks and uncertainty with the patient or appropriate decision-maker. Empirical removal of normal ovaries is not justified merely by a positive antibody. Continue cognitive, psychiatric and functional rehabilitation, because neurologic recovery may lag behind tumor treatment and the disappearance of acute autonomic or seizure complications.

questions.explanation:
Faciobrachial Events Before Memory Decline

Correct answer: Urgent LGI1-focused assessment and consideration of immunotherapy, alongside seizure care

Recognize a Time-Sensitive Warning Phenotype

**Faciobrachial dystonic seizures are very brief, frequent stereotyped events** involving the face and arm, sometimes with leg involvement. They are strongly associated with LGI1 autoimmunity.

They can precede obvious amnesia or a broader limbic syndrome. Normal sodium, MRI or routine EEG early in the course does not exclude the association.

Obtain event videos when possible and review semiology carefully. The term dystonic describes the motor appearance and does not mean these should automatically follow a primary movement-disorder pathway.

Treat the Immune Process as Well as the Events

**Early specialist immune treatment is important when the integrated diagnosis is supported.** The 103-patient observational study associated prompt FBDS cessation with lower subsequent cognitive impairment.

This is clinically persuasive observational evidence rather than a guarantee that treatment prevents every cognitive deficit. Do not wait for established dementia to act on a well-supported early syndrome.

Use appropriate LGI1 testing and assess competing diagnoses while planning treatment. Antiseizure medicines are adjuncts rather than a substitute for immunotherapy. Follow seizure burden, memory, sodium and function separately; apparent cessation of the visible events does not by itself prove that all limbic dysfunction has resolved.

Optimize antiseizure treatment first and defer immune therapy until cognitive impairment appears: Antiseizure drugs may help events, but observational evidence supports treating the immune process early rather than waiting for memory decline in a supported LGI1 phenotype.

Obtain prolonged video-EEG before beginning the neural antibody investigation: Video-EEG can characterize events, but a clear scalp correlate may be absent in FBDS; antibody and specialist immune evaluation should proceed rather than depend on EEG capture.

Use interval MRI to confirm hippocampal injury before considering immune treatment: MRI follow-up can be useful, but a normal early scan does not exclude LGI1-associated FBDS or justify waiting for structural injury before assessment and treatment.

questions.question: A 71-year-old develops subacute amnesia and focal seizures. Sodium is 126 mmol/L with a euvolemic hypotonic pattern. MRI shows medial temporal signal change and CSF has two leukocytes per cubic millimetre. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

Correct sodium first and defer neural antibody testing until cognition is reassessed
Consider LGI1 encephalitis while investigating and treating the sodium disturbance

questions.explanation:
Hyponatremia Can Be a Clue Rather Than the Whole Diagnosis

Correct answer: Consider LGI1 encephalitis while investigating and treating the sodium disturbance

Integrate the Limbic and Systemic Findings

**LGI1 encephalitis commonly affects older adults with memory impairment and focal seizures.** FBDS are particularly helpful when present, but are not required.

Hyponatremia is frequent and can reflect inappropriate antidiuresis. It strengthens suspicion in the appropriate syndrome without identifying the cause by itself.

Routine CSF can be normal or minimally abnormal. Serum testing is often more sensitive for LGI1 than CSF, although paired testing can help the broader assessment.

Manage Sodium and Brain Disease Together

**Assess sodium chronicity, symptoms and contributing medicines**, and correct through an appropriate monitored protocol. Overly rapid correction creates a separate neurologic hazard.

Investigate other causes of hypotonic hyponatremia, including endocrine and drug-related causes. Treating the immune disease does not remove the need for safe electrolyte care.

Monitor cognition and seizure control as sodium improves; persistence of limbic deficits should not be dismissed as delayed electrolyte recovery without reassessment. Use immunotherapy when the integrated evidence supports LGI1 disease and assess tumor risk appropriately, recognizing that this association differs from the much stronger SCLC links of selected other neural antibodies.

Prioritize GABA-B receptor encephalitis because hyponatremia specifically identifies SCLC: GABA-B disease and SCLC can cause this combination, but sodium is nonspecific; the older-adult limbic syndrome also strongly warrants LGI1 assessment.

Correct sodium first and defer neural antibody testing until cognition is reassessed: Electrolyte care is essential, but the focal seizures and limbic pattern warrant parallel etiologic testing rather than waiting to see whether sodium explains everything.

Prioritize a degenerative memory disorder with superimposed metabolic seizures: A degenerative disorder can coexist with metabolic illness, but the subacute limbic course and focal seizures require evaluation for a treatable inflammatory syndrome.

questions.question: A man develops severe insomnia, hallucinations, profuse sweating and fluctuating blood pressure. Examination and EMG demonstrate peripheral nerve hyperexcitability with neuromyotonic discharges. Which syndrome best integrates these findings?
options: CASPR2-associated Morvan syndrome
LGI1-associated limbic encephalitis
Isolated acquired neuromyotonia
NMDAR encephalitis
questions.explanation:
Peripheral Hyperexcitability With Insomnia and Dysautonomia

Correct answer: CASPR2-associated Morvan syndrome

Recognize Central, Autonomic and Peripheral Involvement

**Morvan syndrome combines encephalopathic or sleep symptoms, dysautonomia and peripheral nerve hyperexcitability.** Severe insomnia, hallucinations, sweating and cardiovascular fluctuations are useful clues.

Neuromyotonia can produce cramps, stiffness and visible myokymia. EMG documents characteristic spontaneous motor activity rather than attributing every movement to a central seizure.

CASPR2 is an important antigenic association; antigen-specific testing is more informative than an undifferentiated VGKC-complex result.

Investigate Tumor Association and Treat Both Domains

**Assess for an associated tumor, particularly thymoma**, guided by the phenotype and specialist evaluation. Tumor association is important but not universal.

Use immune treatment when supported, plus symptom-directed therapy for peripheral hyperexcitability and carefully monitored sleep/autonomic complications. Selected membrane-stabilizing medicines can reduce motor symptoms without treating the whole immune process.

Review respiratory function, nutrition and medication adverse effects in severe disease. A patient with isolated neuromyotonia has a different clinical burden from one with Morvan syndrome; documenting the central and autonomic domains guides monitoring and prevents an incomplete symptomatic-only treatment plan. Follow relapse and functional recovery rather than using the antibody result alone as the endpoint.

LGI1-associated limbic encephalitis: LGI1 can cause cognitive disturbance and seizures, but the prominent peripheral neuromyotonia with insomnia and autonomic disturbance particularly suggests the Morvan/CASPR2 spectrum.

Isolated acquired neuromyotonia: Isolated neuromyotonia explains cramps and continuous muscle activity, but not the full encephalopathic, sleep and autonomic syndrome that defines the broader Morvan phenotype.

NMDAR encephalitis: NMDAR disease can cause insomnia, dysautonomia and movements, but EMG-confirmed peripheral neuromyotonia with this combined syndrome more specifically supports Morvan disease.

questions.question: A 63-year-old smoker has new recurrent seizures progressing to status epilepticus with subacute memory loss. CSF and serum testing confirm GABA-B receptor antibodies in a compatible syndrome. Which associated malignancy deserves particular attention?
options: Ovarian teratoma
Small-cell lung carcinoma
Thymoma
Testicular germ-cell tumor
questions.explanation:
Seizure-Predominant Limbic Disease and SCLC Risk

Correct answer: Small-cell lung carcinoma

A Limbic Syndrome With Prominent Seizures

**GABA-B receptor encephalitis often causes severe seizures with limbic cognitive or behavioral dysfunction.** Status epilepticus can dominate the presentation.

MRI and CSF findings vary, and no single imaging appearance substitutes for clinical and antibody integration. Exclude infection and other seizure-related causes as appropriate.

The association with SCLC is substantial, especially in the relevant age and smoking context, but an initially negative tumor search does not negate the neurologic diagnosis.

Coordinate Neurologic and Cancer Care

**Arrange prompt tumor investigation directed toward the chest and the broader clinical context.** Use appropriate imaging and oncologic assessment rather than relying on serum tumor markers alone.

Treat seizures/status and the immune process while evaluating malignancy. When cancer is found, tumor-directed therapy is a central component of the overall plan, not a reason to postpone supportive neurologic care.

Determine repeat screening from the antibody/phenotype risk framework and clinical course. Coexisting antibodies can modify interpretation and prognosis. Counsel that outcome depends on both neurologic injury and tumor factors; control of seizures does not establish cure of the associated cancer or remove the need for cognitive rehabilitation and follow-up.

Ovarian teratoma: Teratoma is a characteristic association in the appropriate NMDAR population, but GABA-B receptor encephalitis in an older smoker particularly raises SCLC risk.

Thymoma: Thymoma is relevant to selected CASPR2 and other autoimmune neurologic syndromes, but SCLC is the characteristic tumor concern with this GABA-B receptor phenotype.

Testicular germ-cell tumor: Germ-cell tumors are important in selected Ma2/KLHL11-associated syndromes, particularly with brainstem or diencephalic features, rather than the leading association here.

questions.explanation:
AMPAR Disease Needs Tumor and Relapse Assessment

Correct answer: Complete phenotype-directed tumor assessment and monitor clinically for relapse and residual deficits

A Limbic Phenotype With Important Cancer Associations

questions.question: A patient with type 1 diabetes and nonspecific dizziness has a low-positive serum GAD65 result. There is no objective stiff-person, cerebellar or epileptic syndrome. Which interpretation is best?
options: The result may reflect endocrine autoimmunity and does not establish a neurologic GAD65 syndrome
Use repeat serum titre progression as the main criterion for neurologic attribution
Use CSF oligoclonal bands as sufficient confirmation of GAD65-mediated disease
Apply a published high-titre cutoff directly after changing its numerical units
questions.explanation:
GAD65 Results Require Assay and Phenotype Context

Correct answer: The result may reflect endocrine autoimmunity and does not establish a neurologic GAD65 syndrome

A Broad Antibody Association, Not a Single Diagnosis

**GAD65 antibodies occur in type 1 diabetes and in selected neurologic syndromes**, including stiff-person spectrum, cerebellar ataxia, epilepsy and limbic encephalitis.

Low serum levels lack specificity for neurologic autoimmunity. A high level increases relevance in a compatible syndrome, but is not independently pathognomonic.

The Mayo radioimmunoassay cohort defined high titre as more than 20 nmol/L. This is an assay-specific research/clinical threshold, not a universal cutoff for ELISA or every laboratory.

Match Laboratory Evidence to Objective Findings

**Review the clinical phenotype, assay and CSF evidence where appropriate.** Intrathecal antibody production or other supporting findings can increase confidence in selected cases.

Exclude alternative causes of ataxia, seizures or stiffness. Coexisting autoimmune disease can explain why an antibody is present without explaining a new neurologic complaint.

Treatment responsiveness varies across GAD65-associated phenotypes, and chronic epilepsy may not respond like an acute neuronal-surface-antibody syndrome. Set objective goals before immunotherapy and reassess benefit against toxicity. Neither a low titre in isolation nor failure to cross another assay’s threshold should replace specialist evaluation when a convincing objective neurologic syndrome is actually present.

Use repeat serum titre progression as the main criterion for neurologic attribution: Serial titres can contribute in established disease, but changing levels alone do not identify a neurologic syndrome when objective clinical findings are absent.

Use CSF oligoclonal bands as sufficient confirmation of GAD65-mediated disease: Bands can support CNS immune activity in an appropriate setting, but are not GAD65-specific and cannot establish the mechanism without a compatible syndrome.

Apply a published high-titre cutoff directly after changing its numerical units: Thresholds depend on assay calibration and methodology, not just arithmetic unit conversion; an unrelated platform cutoff cannot independently confirm neurologic GAD65 autoimmunity.

questions.question: An adult develops substantial weight loss and persistent diarrhea, followed by cognitive change, exaggerated startle, tremor and myoclonus. Infection and common metabolic causes are being evaluated. Which neural antibody syndrome best fits?
options: CASPR2-associated Morvan syndrome
Glycine-receptor-associated PERM
DPPX antibody-associated encephalitis
GAD65-associated stiff-person spectrum
questions.explanation:
Diarrhea Before a Hyperexcitable Encephalopathy

Correct answer: DPPX antibody-associated encephalitis

Connect Enteric and Central Symptoms

**DPPX is an auxiliary protein associated with Kv4.2 potassium channels.** Antibody-associated disease links gastrointestinal symptoms with cognitive or psychiatric change and CNS hyperexcitability.

Diarrhea and weight loss can precede the neurologic syndrome. Tremor, myoclonus, exaggerated startle and seizures are possible manifestations, with variable tempo.

This combination is a clue for targeted testing, not permission to omit ordinary gastrointestinal, infectious, nutritional or neoplastic evaluation.

Confirm the Mechanism and Restore Function

**Use appropriate antibody confirmation within a compatible phenotype**, assessing CSF and imaging according to the wider differential. Review whether apparent jerks are epileptic, myoclonic or stimulus-related.

Provide fluid, electrolyte and nutritional care while specialist immunotherapy is considered. Severe weight loss can materially affect treatment tolerance and rehabilitation.

Reported improvement with immune treatment supports clinical action, but responses and relapse risk vary and evidence largely comes from observational series. Evaluate associated malignancy when indicated by the syndrome and patient context. Follow cognition, startle burden, gait and nutritional recovery separately rather than assuming that resolution of diarrhea proves neurologic remission.

CASPR2-associated Morvan syndrome: Morvan disease combines insomnia, dysautonomia and peripheral neuromyotonia; gastrointestinal prodrome followed by predominantly central hyperexcitability is more characteristic of DPPX here.

Glycine-receptor-associated PERM: PERM can produce marked startle, rigidity and brainstem/autonomic dysfunction, but the prominent diarrheal and weight-loss prodrome particularly suggests DPPX-associated disease.

GAD65-associated stiff-person spectrum: Stiff-person disease can cause stimulus-sensitive spasms and stiffness, but this gastrointestinal-cognitive-hyperexcitable sequence is not its typical defining presentation.

questions.question: An older adult has progressive dysphagia, gait instability, nocturnal stridor, obstructive sleep apnea and complex behaviors during both non-REM and REM sleep. Routine MRI is unrevealing. Which diagnosis deserves targeted consideration?
options: Isolated REM sleep behavior disorder with unrelated dysphagia
Progressive supranuclear palsy
Multiple system atrophy
Anti-IgLON5 disease
questions.explanation:
Sleep-Bulbar Disease Outside a Typical Acute Encephalitis

Correct answer: Anti-IgLON5 disease

Recognize the Sleep and Bulbar Combination

**IgLON5 disease can have a chronic progressive course**, with sleep, bulbar, gait, oculomotor or cognitive manifestations. It need not resemble a conventional rapidly evolving limbic encephalitis.

Parasomnias, abnormal non-REM sleep initiation, obstructive apnea and stridor are important clues. A PSP-like presentation can occur, so a familiar movement-disorder phenotype does not end the differential.

Video-polysomnography and targeted antibody testing can help in the appropriate clinical context. Normal routine MRI does not exclude the disease.

Airway Safety Is an Immediate Priority

**Assess stridor, sleep-disordered breathing and swallowing promptly.** Respiratory and aspiration risks can be urgent even while the etiologic workup remains incomplete.

Coordinate sleep, respiratory, ENT and neurologic expertise according to the findings, with appropriate ventilation or airway interventions when needed.

Specialist immunotherapy can be considered, but responses are variable and cannot be promised from the antibody result alone. The relationship between autoimmunity and neurodegenerative pathology is complex. Track bulbar, respiratory, sleep and functional outcomes over time; do not use a chronic course to dismiss the immune association or use a positive antibody to assume that established disability will fully reverse.

Isolated REM sleep behavior disorder with unrelated dysphagia: Isolated REM behavior disorder can precede a synucleinopathy, but it does not adequately integrate prominent non-REM abnormalities, airway symptoms and progressive bulbar dysfunction.

Progressive supranuclear palsy: PSP can cause gait and bulbar dysfunction and has an IgLON5-like mimic, but the complex mixed sleep disorder with stridor should prompt targeted assessment beyond a degenerative label.

Multiple system atrophy: MSA can cause stridor, autonomic failure and REM behavior disorder, but the broader mixed non-REM/REM sleep phenotype with bulbar involvement is an important IgLON5 clue.

questions.question: A patient with fever, seizures and temporal-lobe abnormalities receives intravenous acyclovir. CSF HSV PCR obtained within the first day of neurologic symptoms is negative, but clinical suspicion remains high. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Increase acyclovir above the standard dose because a negative PCR implies resistance
Stop acyclovir and begin steroid monotherapy for presumed autoimmune disease
Replace intravenous acyclovir with oral valacyclovir while awaiting repeat testing
Continue appropriate acyclovir and arrange repeat CSF HSV PCR with reassessment
questions.explanation:
An Early Negative HSV PCR Does Not Clear the Infection

Correct answer: Continue appropriate acyclovir and arrange repeat CSF HSV PCR with reassessment

Use Timing to Interpret the Negative Result

**An early negative HSV PCR can occur despite infection.** A compatible temporal syndrome warrants repeat sampling and continued treatment while the uncertainty is resolved.

IDSA guidance recommends considering repeat PCR in three to seven days when the syndrome or temporal imaging remains suggestive. Interpret the repeat result alongside clinical evolution and alternative diagnoses.

Neural antibody testing can proceed in parallel, but its pending status should not determine whether a plausible infectious emergency receives treatment.

Give the Correct Route and Protect Kidney Function

**The usual adult regimen with normal renal function is acyclovir ==10 mg/kg IV every eight hours==.** Adjust the dose or interval for renal function and use an appropriate weight-based prescribing protocol.

Maintain suitable hydration, monitor renal function and review nephrotoxic medicines. Acyclovir accumulation can itself produce neurotoxicity, particularly with impaired clearance.

Confirmed HSV encephalitis generally requires a prolonged intravenous course, commonly 14–21 days according to immune status, recovery and specialist guidance. This does not mean every initially suspected case needs the full course if a reliable alternative diagnosis is established. Repeat testing and expert reassessment determine when discontinuation is justified; a single early negative test should not be used as automatic clearance for immunosuppression.

Increase acyclovir above the standard dose because a negative PCR implies resistance: A negative early PCR does not demonstrate antiviral resistance; reassess timing and the differential rather than inferring resistance or increasing exposure without an indication.

Stop acyclovir and begin steroid monotherapy for presumed autoimmune disease: Immune disease remains possible, but an early negative PCR does not reliably exclude HSV in a highly compatible syndrome; stopping coverage prematurely can be harmful.

Replace intravenous acyclovir with oral valacyclovir while awaiting repeat testing: Oral therapy is useful for other herpes indications but is not the established substitute for intravenous treatment of suspected acute HSV encephalitis.

questions.question: A patient has severe, well-supported autoimmune encephalitis after appropriate evaluation of infection and other major mimics. Neural antibody results will take two weeks. No biopsy-sensitive mass lesion is suspected. What is the best treatment approach?
options: Begin azathioprine alone as the acute induction regimen
Defer immune therapy until the antibody identifies a molecular target
Begin appropriate first-line immunotherapy now with monitoring and ongoing diagnostic reassessment
Use antiseizure therapy alone until repeat MRI documents further injury
questions.explanation:
Do Not Wait Weeks for a Delayed Antibody Panel

Correct answer: Begin appropriate first-line immunotherapy now with monitoring and ongoing diagnostic reassessment

Treat on Integrated Evidence

**A compatible syndrome and appropriate exclusion of important mimics can justify acute immunotherapy before antibody results.** Severity, objective findings and the trajectory determine urgency.

Collect relevant serum and CSF samples before treatment where feasible without creating an unsafe delay. Continue to review infection results and emerging discordant findings.

If lymphoma or another biopsy-sensitive mass lesion remains a serious consideration, coordinate tissue strategy before steroids when clinically feasible; this differs from the stated scenario.

Use an Acute Rather Than Maintenance Strategy

**First-line options include high-dose corticosteroids, IVIG and plasma exchange.** Severe disease often warrants combination treatment, individualized to contraindications and local expertise.

Monitor glucose, blood pressure, mental state, infection risk and treatment-specific complications. Provide concurrent respiratory, autonomic, seizure and nutritional care as indicated.

Document objective treatment goals, such as consciousness, seizure burden and functional trajectory, rather than relying on subjective improvement alone. Antibody results can later redirect tumor assessment or treatment mechanism. If the patient worsens, reconsider the diagnosis and complications as well as treatment intensity; empiric treatment does not make the original immune attribution immune to revision.

Begin azathioprine alone as the acute induction regimen: Azathioprine can be a selected maintenance agent, but its delayed effect is unsuitable as sole immediate therapy for severe acute encephalitis.

Defer immune therapy until the antibody identifies a molecular target: Antibodies improve classification and guide later choices, but delayed results should not postpone treatment of severe, sufficiently supported disease after appropriate exclusions.

Use antiseizure therapy alone until repeat MRI documents further injury: Seizure treatment is essential, but does not treat the underlying immune process; waiting for additional structural damage is not a necessary treatment criterion.

Pulse IV methylprednisolone alone as the planned complete induction course
IV rituximab as the sole initial induction treatment
Oral prednisone with azathioprine as the initial induction combination
questions.explanation:
Select a First-Line Regimen for Severe Disease

Correct answer: Pulse IV methylprednisolone plus IVIG or plasma exchange

Use a Defined Acute Course

**The Canadian consensus recommends high-dose steroids with IVIG or plasma exchange for severe disease.** This is consensus-informed practice with limited comparative trial evidence.

Milder presentations can require a different balance, including selected steroid monotherapy with specialist input. Do not transfer one severe-disease regimen to every uncertain encephalopathy.

Consider treatment sequence: plasma exchange can remove recently infused immunoglobulin, so coordinate scheduling when both are used.

Match Treatment to the Patient

**Steroids can worsen hyperglycemia, hypertension, psychiatric symptoms and infection.** IVIG requires attention to thrombotic, renal and volume risks.

Plasma exchange requires suitable access and monitoring for hemodynamic instability, electrolyte changes, bleeding and line complications. These risks influence selection rather than establishing a universally superior option.

Assess clinical response and adverse effects during the course, while continuing supportive care. The exact exchange prescription is individualized by the apheresis service. Persistent deficits immediately after induction do not alone establish treatment failure, but severe deterioration or absent meaningful progress warrants timely specialist reassessment rather than indefinite repetition of the same course.

Treatment | Example acute regimen from Canadian consensus | Key monitoring

IV methylprednisolone | ==1 g daily for five days== | Glucose, BP, mental state, infection

IVIG | ==2 g/kg total over two to five days== | Renal function, thrombosis, fluid status

Plasma exchange | Five exchanges on alternate days over approximately ten days | Access, BP, calcium/electrolytes, bleeding

Pulse IV methylprednisolone alone as the planned complete induction course: Steroid monotherapy can be considered in selected mild or moderate disease, but the Canadian consensus recommends combination first-line therapy for severe disease.

IV rituximab as the sole initial induction treatment: Rituximab is a preferred second-line option for many surface-antibody syndromes, but does not replace the rapid first-line combination recommended in this scenario.

Oral prednisone with azathioprine as the initial induction combination: Oral steroid and azathioprine combinations can have maintenance roles, but delayed-onset azathioprine does not supply the acute severe-disease induction effect sought here.

Complications and diagnostic mimics have been reassessed. Which approach best reflects the 2024 Canadian consensus?
options: Consider second-line treatment now, commonly rituximab for this antibody-mediated syndrome
Continue first-line treatment and defer the second-line decision until week four
Repeat IVIG and make escalation dependent on a falling serum antibody titre
Prefer cyclophosphamide as the next agent for this surface-antibody syndrome
questions.explanation:
Escalation Timing Depends on Severity and Guideline

Correct answer: Consider second-line treatment now, commonly rituximab for this antibody-mediated syndrome

Recognize Guideline-Specific Timing

**The Canadian consensus supports second-line assessment after five to ten days in severe disease that fails to improve or worsens.** For mild or moderate disease it uses a longer two-to-four-week interval.

The 2021 best-practice recommendations describe consideration after two to four weeks without improvement following combined acute therapy. These are not identical time anchors or high-certainty biologic deadlines.

Clinical severity, treatment adequacy, complications and confidence in the diagnosis determine application. Do not interpret slower expected recovery as a reason to ignore ongoing severe disease.

Select and Monitor the Second-Line Agent

**Rituximab is commonly preferred for neuronal-surface-antibody disease.** Example regimens include 1 g IV repeated after two weeks or 375 mg per square metre weekly for four weeks.

Assess infection risks, hepatitis B status, blood counts and immunoglobulins and arrange appropriate infusion precautions before treatment. Drug safety and prevention measures require an individualized plan.

Continue tumor assessment and supportive care. Improvement may lag behind B-cell depletion, and refractory disease can require specialist reassessment of mechanism and further options. Evidence for later agents is more limited; do not present emerging rescue treatments as interchangeable standard care or escalate without checking for infection and treatment-related deterioration.

Continue first-line treatment and defer the second-line decision until week four: A two-to-four-week interval appears in other guidance or less severe settings, but this question specifies the Canadian severe-disease recommendation supporting assessment at five to ten days.

Repeat IVIG and make escalation dependent on a falling serum antibody titre: Additional first-line treatment can be selected, but a titre fall is not a prerequisite for escalation when a severe, well-supported syndrome fails to improve.

Prefer cyclophosphamide as the next agent for this surface-antibody syndrome: Cyclophosphamide has selected refractory or cell-mediated immune indications, but rituximab is generally preferred for NMDAR disease in the cited consensus.

questions.question: Rituximab is planned for severe antibody-mediated encephalitis. HBsAg is negative, but total anti-HBc is positive. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Defer rituximab until anti-HBc becomes negative on repeat serology
Proceed with rituximab and monitor liver enzymes without a virologic prevention plan
Assess prior HBV infection and arrange an expert reactivation-prevention plan before B-cell depletion
Give a hepatitis B vaccine booster and proceed without further HBV assessment
questions.explanation:
HBsAg Alone Is Not Adequate Before Rituximab

Correct answer: Assess prior HBV infection and arrange an expert reactivation-prevention plan before B-cell depletion

Screen for Current and Previous Infection

**Rituximab can reactivate HBV even when HBsAg is negative.** Prescribing information requires HBsAg and anti-HBc testing before treatment.

Interpret anti-HBc with the clinical context and additional serology; seek HBV DNA and specialist advice as appropriate. Anti-HBs positivity does not by itself cancel the concern.

Coordinate antiviral prevention and monitoring with clinicians experienced in HBV. For high-risk B-cell-depleting treatment, do not substitute liver-enzyme surveillance alone for an appropriate prevention strategy.

Plan Safety Beyond One Screening Test

**Review active infections, blood counts and baseline immunoglobulins**, and assess vaccination and other prevention needs in the context of urgency and prior therapy.

Monitor infusion reactions and later infectious complications. Prolonged steroid combinations can require additional infection prevention based on dose, duration and patient risks.

HBV exposure is not automatically a permanent prohibition against rituximab; it requires a concrete risk-reduction plan. Document who will prescribe and monitor antiviral care and how follow-up continues after immune treatment, because reactivation can be delayed. Balance the neurologic urgency against modifiable infection risks through coordinated specialist decisions rather than overlooking a positive core antibody.

Defer rituximab until anti-HBc becomes negative on repeat serology: Anti-HBc can remain positive after prior infection; waiting for seroreversion is not the appropriate safety endpoint when expert antiviral prevention can enable necessary treatment.

Proceed with rituximab and monitor liver enzymes without a virologic prevention plan: Liver monitoring is useful, but negative HBsAg does not remove reactivation risk from prior infection and enzyme surveillance alone is inadequate high-risk planning.

Give a hepatitis B vaccine booster and proceed without further HBV assessment: Vaccination protects susceptible patients from new infection but does not eliminate latent-virus reactivation risk in someone with evidence of previous infection.

questions.question: A patient with severe NMDAR encephalitis develops fluctuating consciousness, recurrent apnea and marked heart-rate and BP variability. Which immediate care plan is most appropriate?
options: Use supplemental oxygen alone and assess ventilation if saturation falls
Escalate immunotherapy on the ward and await a respiratory response
ICU-level respiratory and hemodynamic support while continuing mechanism-directed treatment
Treat all observed movements with escalating anesthetic antiseizure therapy
questions.explanation:
Hypoventilation Requires Organ Support During Immune Treatment

Correct answer: ICU-level respiratory and hemodynamic support while continuing mechanism-directed treatment

Support Physiology While Immune Therapy Takes Effect

**Central hypoventilation and dysautonomia can be life-threatening in NMDAR encephalitis.** Recurrent apnea warrants urgent airway and ventilatory assessment.

Monitor ventilation as well as oxygenation. Heart-rate and BP instability require continuous assessment, attention to provoking factors and appropriately titrated treatment.

Review sedation, medicines, infection and seizures as additional causes of deterioration; do not attribute every new abnormality automatically to autoimmune activity.

Prevent Complications of a Prolonged Admission

**Coordinate seizure monitoring, aspiration prevention and nutrition**, with thrombosis prevention, pressure care and safe mobilization when feasible.

Use video-EEG to distinguish seizures from complex dyskinesias when uncertainty changes management. Avoid unnecessary sedative accumulation while controlling dangerous agitation and confirmed status.

Continue immune and tumor-directed care alongside organ support rather than treating these as sequential stages. Communication with family and rehabilitation planning are important during a potentially long recovery. Severe initial illness does not prove irreversible injury, but prolonged immobility, infection and treatment toxicity can add disability if preventive care is neglected. Reassess readiness for weaning and functional participation as consciousness and autonomic stability improve.

Use supplemental oxygen alone and assess ventilation if saturation falls: Oxygen can improve saturation while hypoventilation and hypercapnia persist; recurrent apnea requires direct ventilation assessment and appropriate airway support.

Escalate immunotherapy on the ward and await a respiratory response: Immunotherapy treats the underlying disease but cannot be relied on to reverse recurrent apnea immediately; airway and circulatory risks need monitored organ support.

Treat all observed movements with escalating anesthetic antiseizure therapy: Confirmed status can require anesthetic treatment, but dyskinesias and autonomic events are not all seizures; EEG correlation helps avoid unnecessary suppression and additional respiratory harm.

questions.question: Six months after LGI1 encephalitis, a patient has stable residual memory difficulty. A week of poor sleep and a sedating medicine is followed by worse attention, without clear new seizures or focal findings. Which next approach is best?
options: Give another acute IVIG course and interpret improvement as confirmation of relapse

Measure serum antibody titre and escalate if it remains positive
Continue the current medicines and monitor cognition at the next routine annual visit
questions.explanation:
Residual Memory Problems Are Not Automatically Relapse

Correct answer: Assess medicines, sleep, seizures and objective change before assigning relapse or escalating immunotherapy

Separate Recovery, Fluctuation and New Inflammation

**Cognitive, sleep, mood and seizure problems can persist after autoimmune encephalitis.** Stable residual disability does not necessarily mean ongoing immune activity.

Define the baseline and time course and seek collateral history. Review medicines, sleep, infection, metabolic factors and possible seizures; select EEG, MRI or CSF when the clinical question warrants them.

Use serial objective cognitive and functional assessment where possible. A single symptom report or antibody level cannot independently establish relapse.

Individualize Long-Term Immune Treatment

**A convincing clinical relapse with appropriate supporting evidence can justify acute retreatment and maintenance planning.** Recurrent disease differs from a monophasic episode with residual deficits.

Balance relapse risk against infection, hypogammaglobulinemia and other treatment toxicity. There is no universally proven maintenance regimen or duration for every antibody syndrome.

Provide cognitive rehabilitation, mood and sleep treatment, and support for work, driving and daily activities according to function. Continue appropriate cancer follow-up when relevant. Improvement in reversible contributors can reduce disability without immune escalation; persistent objective deterioration after those factors are addressed should prompt renewed assessment rather than an indefinite assumption that recovery alone explains it.

Give another acute IVIG course and interpret improvement as confirmation of relapse: A supported relapse may require treatment, but nonspecific improvement cannot establish the cause; medicines, sleep and seizures should first be assessed in this scenario.

Measure serum antibody titre and escalate if it remains positive: Persistent antibodies can accompany recovery or residual injury, so positivity alone cannot distinguish relapse from the reversible contributors described.

Continue the current medicines and monitor cognition at the next routine annual visit: Longitudinal follow-up is useful, but a new change with identifiable medicine and sleep factors deserves timely reassessment rather than passive annual observation.

questions.question: A patient with a high-risk neurologic phenotype has a confirmed high-risk neural antibody. Initial cancer investigation is negative. Which principle best reflects the 2021 PNS-Care framework?
options: Any coincident tumor establishes definite PNS regardless of its type
A high-risk antibody establishes definite PNS independently of cancer findings
Negative initial screening excludes a paraneoplastic mechanism
Integrate phenotype, antibody, cancer evidence and follow-up rather than declaring definite PNS from the antibody alone
questions.explanation:
PNS Certainty Requires Integrated Evidence

Correct answer: Integrate phenotype, antibody, cancer evidence and follow-up rather than declaring definite PNS from the antibody alone

Use the Framework Rather Than One Positive Test

**PNS-Care combines the clinical phenotype, neural antibody risk and evidence of a relevant cancer.** Follow-up can change diagnostic certainty when an initially occult tumor is later detected.

The 2021 score categories are definite at eight or more, probable at six to seven, possible at four to five and non-PNS by this classification at three or less.

These categories standardize certainty rather than replacing clinical judgment. A low score does not itself explain the symptoms or make further investigation unnecessary when suspicion remains.

Exclude Competing Cancer-Related Mechanisms

**Direct metastasis, leptomeningeal disease, treatment toxicity, infection and metabolic disturbance must be considered.** Cancer plus neurologic symptoms is not automatically an immune PNS.

Confirm unexpected antibody results with appropriate laboratory methods and correlate their known phenotype and tumor associations.

Plan cancer assessment from the integrated risk profile and revisit it as follow-up accumulates. A new tumor diagnosis can increase certainty, while prolonged negative surveillance can alter the classification. Record the current evidence and uncertainty rather than preserving an initial label indefinitely; clinical care and symptom treatment should continue while the etiologic status is reassessed.

Any coincident tumor establishes definite PNS regardless of its type: A coincident tumor can be unrelated; phenotype-antibody-tumor consistency and, in selected discordant cases, antigen expression matter to attribution.

A high-risk antibody establishes definite PNS independently of cancer findings: High-risk antibodies strongly guide tumor investigation, but the framework combines clinical, antibody and cancer evidence; antibody positivity alone does not establish definite PNS.

Negative initial screening excludes a paraneoplastic mechanism: Neurologic disease can precede detection of cancer, so a negative initial search does not end appropriate high-risk surveillance.

questions.question: Which comparison best explains why an anti-Hu syndrome may respond differently to antibody-removal treatment than NMDAR encephalitis?
options: Hu and NMDAR antibodies primarily cause the same reversible surface-receptor internalization
Hu targets an intracellular antigen and often marks T-cell-associated injury, whereas NMDAR surface antibodies can directly alter receptor function
Hu is a surface channel antibody while NMDAR is an intracellular marker
Hu-associated disease is a direct metastatic complication while NMDAR disease is immune-mediated
questions.explanation:
Intracellular Antibodies Often Mark a Cellular Immune Process

Correct answer: Hu targets an intracellular antigen and often marks T-cell-associated injury, whereas NMDAR surface antibodies can directly alter receptor function

Antigen Location Informs Mechanism

**Many classical intracellular onconeural antibodies are biomarkers of a predominantly cellular immune response.** They can be highly informative for cancer search without being the sole direct effector of neuronal injury.

Neuronal-surface antibodies, such as NMDAR IgG, can directly disturb synaptic function. Selected syndromes can therefore show substantial recovery when immune activity is controlled.

This distinction is a framework, not a guarantee of response or a rule covering every intracellular antigen; GAD65-associated disease needs its own phenotype-specific interpretation.

Set Realistic Treatment Goals

**Tumor-directed treatment is central when a relevant malignancy is present.** Specialist immune treatment may aim to stabilize disease before irreversible neuronal loss accumulates.

Apheresis or IVIG should not be assumed to reverse established anti-Hu neuronal loss as readily as a reversible surface-receptor dysfunction. Conversely, limited expected reversibility does not justify abandoning supportive care.

Assess progression, function and complications and discuss the evidence limits of immune options. Rehabilitation, pain and autonomic care remain important even when complete recovery is unlikely. Do not infer either therapeutic futility or a mandatory drug solely from antibody location; use the clinical syndrome, cancer status and treatment risks.

Feature | Classical intracellular onconeural syndromes | Neuronal-surface-antibody syndromes

Examples | Hu, Yo, Ma2 | NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2

Mechanistic framework | Often predominantly cellular injury; antibody is an important marker | Antibody-mediated disruption of accessible targets can be important

Cancer interpretation | Many have high cancer association; target-specific search | Cancer risk varies considerably by antibody and patient

Treatment implication | Tumor control is central; established neuronal loss may limit reversal | Immune therapy can reverse dysfunction, but recovery is not guaranteed

Hu and NMDAR antibodies primarily cause the same reversible surface-receptor internalization: NMDAR antibodies can alter surface receptor availability, but Hu is intracellular and the associated injury is not explained by the same surface-antibody mechanism.

Hu is a surface channel antibody while NMDAR is an intracellular marker: This reverses the target locations and would mislead both mechanistic reasoning and expectations for immune treatment.

Hu-associated disease is a direct metastatic complication while NMDAR disease is immune-mediated: Hu-associated PNS is immune-mediated despite its cancer association; direct metastatic disease is a separate mechanism that must be excluded.

questions.question: A 68-year-old smoker develops a subacute painful, asymmetric, non-length-dependent sensory syndrome with marked sensory ataxia and reduced sensory nerve action potentials. Anti-Hu is confirmed. Which tumor should be prioritized?
options: Thymoma
Small-cell lung carcinoma
Ovarian teratoma
Hodgkin lymphoma
questions.explanation:
Anti-Hu Sensory Neuronopathy Directs the Cancer Search

Correct answer: Small-cell lung carcinoma

Recognize a Sensory Ganglion Pattern

**Sensory neuronopathy can be asymmetric and non-length-dependent**, affecting upper limbs or trunk early and producing severe proprioceptive ataxia.

Electrophysiology can show reduced sensory responses without the usual distal gradient. Assess strength and other neurologic domains because anti-Hu disease can be multifocal.

Sjogren disease, selected toxins and other immune or inherited disorders are alternative causes of neuronopathy; the confirmed antibody and clinical risk context refine this case.

Search and Follow According to Risk

**Arrange prompt chest-focused and appropriate broader cancer evaluation.** A normal first study does not end the search in a high-risk phenotype-antibody combination.

Coordinate additional imaging and tissue diagnosis with the relevant services; tumor markers alone cannot exclude SCLC. Treat an identified malignancy and consider specialist immune therapy in parallel.

Provide fall prevention, gait aids, neuropathic pain and autonomic assessment where relevant. Established ganglion-cell injury may recover incompletely, so stabilization and preservation of remaining function are meaningful goals. Reassess atypical progression for another process rather than attributing every later symptom to the original neuronopathy.

Thymoma: Thymoma is important in selected CASPR2-associated disease and other immune syndromes, but anti-Hu sensory neuronopathy particularly directs attention toward SCLC.

Ovarian teratoma: Teratoma is a characteristic NMDAR association in an appropriate population, but is not the leading tumor concern in an older smoker with confirmed anti-Hu neuronopathy.

Hodgkin lymphoma: Hodgkin lymphoma is associated with DNER/Tr-related cerebellar disease among other presentations; the antibody and sensory-ganglion phenotype here more strongly favor SCLC.

questions.question: A patient has a high-risk neurologic phenotype and a confirmed high-risk antibody. A comprehensive initial tumor search is negative. What repeat-screening schedule does the 2021 PNS consensus recommend for this combination?
options: Repeat tumor screening every four to six months for two years
Repeat tumor screening every four to six months for one year
Repeat tumor screening every twelve months for two years
Repeat tumor screening every four to six months for five years
questions.explanation:
Repeat Screening in a High-Risk Combination

Correct answer: Repeat tumor screening every four to six months for two years

Apply the Schedule to the Right Population

**The 2021 PNS consensus recommends repeat screening every ==four to six months for two years==** after a negative initial investigation in patients with both high-risk phenotypes and high-risk antibodies.

The schedule is risk-stratified. It should not be copied automatically to every isolated low-risk antibody result or every patient with nonspecific neurologic symptoms.

Some additional situations warrant individualized surveillance according to demographic risk, antibody, phenotype and clinical evolution. Document the rationale rather than assuming one schedule is universal.

Choose Investigations From the Expected Tumor Spectrum

**Repeat assessment should remain directed by the syndrome and antibody.** Review whether the initial studies adequately evaluated the relevant organs and whether another modality or specialist review is needed.

Do not rely on normal tumor markers alone. Conversely, repeated low-yield whole-body testing without a clinical risk framework can create incidental findings and unnecessary procedures.

Maintain neurologic treatment and rehabilitation while surveillance continues. A newly detected compatible tumor changes diagnostic confidence and treatment planning; a discordant tumor requires careful attribution rather than automatic PNS labeling. At the end of the planned period, reassess the clinical course and evidence instead of promising that no future cancer is possible.

Repeat tumor screening every four to six months for one year: This uses the appropriate interval but truncates the two-year surveillance period recommended for the stated high-risk phenotype-antibody combination.

Repeat tumor screening every twelve months for two years: Annual assessment is used in some different follow-up frameworks, but the 2021 PNS consensus specifies a shorter four-to-six-month interval for this combination.

Repeat tumor screening every four to six months for five years: Longer individualized surveillance may be justified in selected cases, but five years is not the specified standard duration of this 2021 recommendation.

questions.question: A patient with cancer and a prior immune neurologic diagnosis develops new multifocal radicular pain, cranial neuropathies and worsening gait. Which next approach is best?
options: Increase immunosuppression because new neurologic symptoms establish PNS progression
Reassess for direct cancer involvement, treatment toxicity, infection and metabolic causes before assigning immune relapse
Use a persistent neural antibody as the principal discriminator of immune relapse
Attribute the symptoms to chemotherapy and assess response after the next cycle
questions.explanation:
Cancer Does Not Make Every Neurologic Syndrome Paraneoplastic

Correct answer: Reassess for direct cancer involvement, treatment toxicity, infection and metabolic causes before assigning immune relapse

Reopen the Mechanism When the Pattern Changes

**A cancer patient can have several neurologic mechanisms over time.** Metastasis, leptomeningeal disease, coagulopathy, treatment toxicity, infection and metabolic disturbance can coexist with PNS.

Define the new localization and tempo, review treatments and immune suppression, and select contrast imaging and safe CSF assessment according to the suspected process.

A previous correct immune diagnosis does not guarantee that each later symptom has the same cause. New pain, cranial deficits or systemic features can change the priorities.

Target Treatment to the Reassessed Cause

**Coordinate neurologic and oncology review**, using microbiology, cytology or other tests when indicated rather than treating the antibody as the endpoint of investigation.

A negative initial cytology may need optimized repeat sampling when leptomeningeal suspicion remains; infection and bleeding risks influence procedure timing.

Treat urgent threats and provide symptom support while evidence is assembled. Immune escalation can worsen an unrecognized infection and does not adequately treat direct malignant spread. Conversely, finding a treatment-related contributor does not automatically exclude simultaneous immune activity. Document the evidence for each proposed mechanism and reassess response against objective clinical findings.

Increase immunosuppression because new neurologic symptoms establish PNS progression: An immune relapse is possible, but this pattern also raises direct leptomeningeal involvement and other actionable mechanisms that require targeted assessment.

Use a persistent neural antibody as the principal discriminator of immune relapse: An antibody may persist and does not independently distinguish direct cancer spread, treatment injury or infection from renewed immune activity.

Attribute the symptoms to chemotherapy and assess response after the next cycle: Treatment toxicity is relevant, but cranial and radicular progression can signal direct malignant or infectious involvement; continuing therapy without evaluation may delay appropriate care.
